title: 13th month pay gift ideas: new home business ventures
summary: With the economy the way it is, maybe a 13th month holiday gift (to yourself?) should be something you can eventually monetize? In the past, fabrication was left to the warehouses and workshops. But…

blocks.text: With the economy the way it is, maybe a 13th month holiday gift (to yourself?) should be something you can eventually monetize? In the past, fabrication was left to the warehouses and workshops. But with advancements in technology, you can turn your home office into a workshop with these two gift ideas: a laser cutter and a 3D printer.
Bambu Lab P2S with AMS 2 Pro Combo
My outlook on some aspects of my life literally changed when I acquired my 3D printer. Whenever I see small furnishings and knick knacks, I go “hey I can print that for a fraction of the price!”

For my birthday I got myself a Bambu Lab P2S with an AMS 2 Pro combo set. You see, I had been mulling over a 3D printer for years, but was quickly dissuaded because my friends who had one often told me that they were doing more maintenance and troubleshooting more than printing. But that has changed in the past few years with the advent of more mature 3D printing machines that don’t break so you can focus on the joys of printing plastic.

For the Philippine weather I opted for an enclosed system as things like humidity and heat management are key to keeping prints stable. I ended up choosing the P2S because it had the latest software and UI compared to the previous P1S model. This means that the P2S was essentially a “next generation” platform that had loads of improvements in both quality control and UI.
I can print that!

As a fan of collectible card games like Magic: The Gathering, I wanted to print out my own custom deck boxes for myself and to give away to friends. I’ve also been very hyper-sentitive lately with the accessories I see for sale in Facebook Marketplace, that some of the open source print designs I see are actually being sold by other printers. So why not just print them myself right?

If you’re going into business, the P2S with the AMS 2 Pro seems to be the ‘modern’ starting point for many as it is more or less a “print and forget” device. The enclosed system with printer and AMS for humidity control (the first thing I printed out were desiccant holders to keep humidity below 30%) keep things plug and play. I now just spend my money buying PLA filament from stores like Maker Lab.

Although I don’t really intend to go into business, pricing your prints is fairly simple as the Bambu Studio app shows the filament used per print. I have a mental computation in my head knowing that 1 kilo of PLA filament is usually around P 600-750 so I divide the cost by the amount of filament used and add a markup for labor.

As mentioned, the things I print are mostly cases for my hobby, but I’ve printed Christmas decor, tea lights, gadget holders, and IKEA-compatible Skadis mounts for my room. Overall, I think the benefits of a 3D printer – even without an eye to turn it into a business – can be really beneficial as I can now make bespoke furniture and crafts to fit my needs.

blocks.caption: The xTool M2 is a laser cutter and printer rolled into one. You can use it to cut wood, paper, and other medium like plastic and metal.

blocks.text: The xTool M2 was a daunting unboxing. I knew I was dealing with a heavy duty machine after watching the fire safety video to unlock the device functions during setup. Unfettered, I wanted sallied forth to make this tool work because I’ve seen the many amazing things it can do with wood, as well as other media.

The xTool M2 is several devices in one. And for roughly P40,xxx, it’s a steal for what it can do (the current holiday sale puts this device down to P36,xxx). It’s primarily a laser cutter and engraver. It’s used to cut and engrave wood to fabricate ornaments and customized giveaways. The wooden coasters I see in bazaars with your initials – that’s most probably made using an xTool unit. But again, I wanted to fabricate things for my hobby. So rather than just cutting shapes, I wanted to assemble a trading card deck box made from 3mm basswood. The maker market is alive in online shops so I was able to find basswood boards in Shopee.

blocks.caption: Printing before cutting: switching from printer head to laser cutter for making playing cards.

blocks.text: Cutting on a 20W laser

Setting up the laser parameters was a bit daunting at first because I had to keep in mind things like laser power and speed, which apparently affect how deep or dark the cuts are, depending on the medium. For the deck box, the files were already available on xTool’s social discovery app called Atomm. All I needed to do was look for a design I liked, downloaded it, and let the machine do its thing. I’m still light years ahead of customizing my own designs so in the meantime this will do.

blocks.caption: A laser engraving done on 3mm basswood

blocks.text: The laser cutter is a sight to behold when at work: it’s best to place the xTool by a window where the built-in exhaust pipe can let the smoke out. Remember, the laser is literally heating wood so there will be that burnt smell that permeates your workshop. The deck box cutout roughly took 10 minutes of work with two wooden slabs. In the future, I will need to learn how to maximize space for cutting so that I can reuse the medium.

blocks.caption: Printing and cutting on sticker paper

blocks.text: User generated content

The Atomm site is filled with community generated projects, from Christmas decor, to storage boxes, to board game pieces, and custom engraving templates. For a beginner, this is a treasure trove of thousands of templates you can make, both with the laser cutter and the printer module.

Speaking of the printer module, yes the xTool M2 is also a printer and cutter! Apart from making wooden engravings and decor, the xTool can also print and cut paper. This is great for making custom stickers for giveaways.

blocks.caption: Some custom MTG vampire tokens printed and cut with the XTool M2

blocks.text: For a quick project, I opened Gemini and turned my son’s photo into a sticker pack. I was able to download and export the file into the xTool’s desktop app. The device comes with a camera on the lid that takes a photo of the entire project. I think this is where the on-device AI really shines because it can accurately tell where images end into blank space, vis a vis the size of the wood.

Essentially, the software takes a photo of the medium and applies the software layer on top of it, so I can “paint” and customize sizing and locations of the stickers (or other media I want to print and cut).

blocks.caption: Cut and assembled MTG deck box

blocks.text: The app has a built-in template feature for printing and cutting. All I have to do is manually attach the CMYK printer module via USB and magnets and then replace it with the 20W laser module once the print job finishes. Exchanging the modules is easy.
While setting up, I easily overlooked having to attach the printer cover receptacle, which you need to screw down on the upper left side of the device.
I was able to print custom stickers on sticker paper, with a cut-out following the outline of the art, and was also able to make custom Magic: The Gathering tokens for use in my gaming pod.
I think the xTool M2 really opens up a world of possibilities with what you can create at home.
A return of investment

Even if you aren’t looking to ROI these devices, it can be used in every party or gathering to make custom trinkets. No need to look for your child’s name at a store for a birthday topper – simply print or engrave it out. Looking for a perfect-fitting grid organizer for your drawer? No need to search online shops and guess the actual dimensions! You can just open up a parametric design project and input your LxW and the 3D printer can print a custom grid for you!

blocks.caption: On the left is a laser cut deck box made out of 3.0mm basswood while on the right is a 3D printed goth-inspired deck case made from marble PLA.
